title: The fall (CCC 390, 404–405)
hookLine: a wound handed down to all, a loss of original holiness

lines: NOBODY TEACHES A TODDLER TO GRAB.
WHERE DOES THE LEAN COME FROM?
cards: You promised yourself you wouldn't say it, and you said it. You meant to be patient, and the moment the kid spilled the juice, you weren't.
Paul, writing to the Romans, describes it: the good he wants to do, he doesn't do, and the thing he hates, he does. Nobody has to teach a toddler to grab. Nobody takes a class in resentment.
Something in people leans the wrong way before they've chosen anything. The Church has a name for that lean, and a story for where it came from. Today: the fall.

teach.b: First, the story. In Genesis 3, the first man and woman live in friendship with God in the garden. The serpent asks a question that plants doubt, and they reach for the one fruit they were told to leave.

Then they hide. The Catechism says the account uses figurative language, but tells of a real event at the beginning of human history: the first people chose themselves over God. Second, what was lost.
The Church calls it original holiness and justice: harmony with God, inside the person, between man and woman, and with creation.
Paul sums it up in the Douay-Rheims: "Wherefore as by one man sin entered into this world, and by sin death."
Third, original sin, the Catechism teaches, is contracted, not committed: a state people are born into, not a personal fault. No baby is guilty of anything it chose.
Fourth, human nature is not totally corrupted. It is wounded: weakened in its powers, subject to ignorance, suffering and death, and inclined to sin. That inclination has an old name, concupiscence.
Christians describe this in different ways: Orthodox Christians often speak of ancestral sin, many Reformed Protestants of a deeper corruption of nature, and the Catholic Church says wounded.
And on Easter night, the Church sings an old Latin hymn that dares to call Adam's sin a happy fault, felix culpa, because of the one it brought to the rescue.
So the Catholic story isn't about how bad people are, but about a wound that can be healed.

how: Catholics are taught that baptism takes away original sin, while its wound, the inclination to sin, remains, and they turn to confession and grace for healing throughout life. The Exsultet, with its felix culpa, is sung at the Easter Vigil.

o: a sin so serious it can never be forgiven
a wound inherited from the start, not a personal act
the first wrong thing each person does as a child

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: original sin means every baby personally did something wrong
the Catechism says it's contracted, not committed: a state, not a personal act.
Catholic teaching says human nature is totally corrupted
the Church's word is wounded: weakened and inclined to sin, but not totally corrupted.
the Catechism says Genesis 3 uses figurative language about a real event
it holds both: figurative language, and a real first choice at the beginning of history.

games.q: you're the first man and woman. you've just eaten the fruit, and you hear God walking in the garden. what do you do?
o: leave the garden on your own.
games.why: they hide. the first thing sin does in the story is break the friendship: they're afraid of the one who made them.

practice: Look at one weakness of yours, a place where you lean the wrong way again and again, the way a good doctor looks at a wound: honestly, and with care, without defending it or beating yourself up.
Then look the same way at someone else's weakness, one that grates on you. If you pray, you can ask for healing, for them and for you.

wordCard.voice: Original sin. Not a sin you committed, but a wound handed down to every human being from the beginning: the loss of original holiness, and a lean toward sin. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: original sin, the term Augustine made standard in the West.

carryVoice: Your line: wounded, not ruined. True of everyone, you included. Day three hundred two, done.

sources.q: Wherefore as by one man sin entered into this world, and by sin death.
